title: Hymn and Harvest
premise: Jude Delacroix hosts a late-night call-in show whose callers all turn out to be people who died the previous week, and he has spent ten years rationalizing it as grief, coincidence, or prank. When every photograph from his late grandmother's house begins showing an empty chair that no one remembers, Jude realizes the harvest-song his family sang at supper was never a lullaby but an invitation, and that his grandmother's death last week has made him next. Guided by a found family of fellow 'listeners' who each survived their own verse, he must learn the song's final verse without singing along—because singing it completes the invitation and takes him to the chair. In the end, Jude refuses to sing alone; instead he broadcasts the verse to thousands of living voices so the song is sung by everyone and belongs to no one, breaking the harvest, though he loses his own memories of the found family as the price of survival.
about_author: Vesper Thackeray is the pen name of a former overnight radio producer who spent years answering calls that came in after sign-off. They write horror about small towns, old songs, and the things families agree not to mention.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: POV Jude. On the tenth anniversary of taking over the 2 a.m. slot, Jude fields a call from Mrs. Okonkwo—who died Tuesday—and tells himself, as always, that grief makes listeners strange. The emotional beat is brittle denial: Jude's humor on air versus the shaking hands under the desk.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: POV Jude. Sorting his grandmother's house after her funeral, Jude finds that every photo—from 1953 onward—now includes a wooden chair no one recognizes, always facing the camera. His cousin Renata sees nothing unusual. Beat: dread crystallizing into certainty that something has noticed him.

chapters.title: Callers
chapters.summary: POV Jude, with interludes of caller transcripts. Three dead callers in one night describe the same dream: a long table, a song, a seat being pulled out. One whispers, 'Don't learn the last verse.' Beat: isolation cracking as Jude realizes the calls are warnings, not hauntings.

chapters.title: The Listeners' Choir
chapters.summary: POV Jude. A caller gives an address; Jude finds Marisol, Theo, and Auntie Bess—people who each heard the song and survived by refusing a verse. They form a wary, warm circle over burnt coffee. Beat: found family offered, and Jude's terror of needing anyone.

chapters.title: What Grandma Sang
chapters.summary: POV Marisol. Researching the Delacroix family hymnal, Marisol uncovers that the harvest song predates the town and that every generation one Delacroix 'goes quiet.' Jude hums the melody without realizing. Beat: tenderness shadowed by betrayal—the lullaby was a leash.

chapters.title: Verse Four
chapters.summary: POV Jude. The chair appears in photographs taken yesterday, closer each time. Jude dreams the first four verses fully for the first time and wakes with the tune stuck in his head, unable to stop humming. Beat: the price of survival becomes literal—memory beginning to fray at the edges.

chapters.title: The Empty Broadcast
chapters.summary: POV Theo. While Jude sleeps, the station goes live on its own; four minutes of a cappella harmony airs, and by morning three listeners are missing. Theo covers for Jude and lies to the others about how bad it is. Beat: guilt, protectiveness, the group fracturing under fear.

chapters.title: Renata's Supper
chapters.summary: POV Jude. At a family dinner, Renata serves the old recipe and leads the song; everyone sings including, helplessly, Jude—verses one through five. The chair is now in the room, real, pulled slightly from the table. Beat: catastrophe through love; the trap was always affection.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: POV Jude, climax. In the broadcast booth at 2 a.m., the dead callers sing the final verse together, offering it like a gift. Jude learns it—every note—but keeps his mouth closed while Marisol, Theo, and Bess hold the line open to the whole listening city. Beat: terror transfigured into defiance.

chapters.title: Everyone Sings
chapters.summary: POV Marisol, resolution. Thousands of strangers sing the last verse at once, and the song, belonging to everyone, belongs to no one; the chair burns to ash in an empty house. Jude survives but cannot remember the faces of the people who saved him—they visit anyway, starting again. Beat: grief and grace; found family chosen twice.
